summary.text: 爱 means “love” or “be fond of.” Its current form is 爫 above 冖 and 友; one proposed graphic account traces the lower shape to joined or abbreviated 心-and-夂 strokes in running script.

formation.text: The received analysis of 愛 treats it as 夊 plus phonetic 㤅. Accounts of the earlier 㤅 graph identify its upper element differently: 兂 in one account, 旡 in others, with 既 also discussed as a variant. The precise graphic sequence remains unsettled.

components.text: In current 爱, 爫 is the visible upper component; its presence identifies the shape but does not establish a historical meaning or sound role.
In current 爱, 冖 is the visible middle component. It is structural here; the evidence does not assign it an independent historical role.
友 is the visible lower component in 爱’s current structure. Its resemblance does not establish an ancient meaning or sound role in 愛.
Early 㤅 uses 心 as a meaning element for benevolence or feeling; this component belongs to the historical graph, not modern 爱.

One analysis identifies the upper element of early 㤅 as 兂 and assigns it a proposed sound role; competing accounts identify 旡, and one discusses 既 variants. This component record represents the disputed 兂 analysis.

sound_limitation.text: The current readings do not resolve whether the historical upper element was 兂 or 旡, or establish an ancient sound relationship.

sound.text: One analysis proposes 兂 as a sound element in 㤅. Their current Mandarin readings are zān and ài; this comparison does not establish the historical relationship.
Other accounts identify the upper element as 旡. Its current Mandarin reading, jì, differs from 㤅 ài; this comparison does not establish the historical relationship.

components.text: In the received analysis of 愛, 夊 is the walking-related element, matching the gloss “appearance of walking”; 㤅 supplies the sound element. This is a historical analysis of 愛, not a role in current 爱.

sound.text: 夊 is read suī and 愛 is read ài in Modern Mandarin. This current-reading comparison does not establish an ancient sound role in 愛.

history.text: No historical glyph was selected or verified. The cited book scan contains the 愛(爱) entry, but is not an image of a historical glyph; the adjacent page begins a different entry rather than continuing 愛.

Accounts of early 愛 distinguish the 㤅 graph from forms analyzed as 愛 with an added 夂 or 夊. One account identifies the upper element of 㤅 as 兂; others identify it as 旡, and another discusses 既 variants. These are competing analyses and regional graphic histories, not one established universal sequence.
爱 is described as a cursive-derived regularization of 愛 and was officially adopted in 1956; that adoption date does not establish when the shape first arose.

uncertainties.text: Accounts disagree about the upper element in early 㤅: one identifies 兂, while others identify 旡; another also discusses 既 variants. No verified same-system historical pronunciation pair settles either the element’s identity or its proposed sound role.

Early 㤅 is glossed as benevolence, while the Shuowen tradition glosses 愛 as an appearance of walking; later examples use 愛 for affection. How and when 愛 took on that affection-related use remains unresolved.

Proposed connections between the spoken word 愛 and other Sino-Tibetan words, and a separate proposal linking it with breath or inhalation vocabulary, remain disputed hypotheses about the word rather than explanations of the graph.

senses.text: Transmitted literary passages use 愛 for affection, including examples in the Zuozhuan and Classic of Poetry. A Guodian 老子甲 transcription reads “甚愛必大費”; a separate book account reports a 㤅(愛) spelling there and interprets 㤅 as used like 愛. The book also reports a Zhongshan bronze example “慈㤅(愛)”. These Warring States examples are source reports, not artifact readings independently verified here, and the transmitted texts do not establish the earliest physical witness or when 愛 acquired this use.
Modern 爱 means love, affection, fondness, and liking; 愛 is its traditional counterpart. The evidence supports these current senses but does not establish a dated sequence among them.

limitations.text: Early 㤅 is associated with benevolence, while later examples use 愛 for affection. The transition is not securely dated, and the evidence does not settle whether it involved borrowing, replacement, or another process; no development is asserted.

relationships.text: In early 㤅, 心 contributes the heart or feeling category.

One analysis identifies 兂 as the proposed sound element in early 㤅; competing accounts identify 旡, with 既 also discussed as a variant. No verified historical pronunciation comparison establishes the sound relationship.
爱 is the officially adopted simplified form of 愛; its shape is described as cursive-derived regularization.
Early bronze forms of 愛 are described as 㤅, while Qin-type forms add 夊. This connects 㤅 to 愛’s graphic history without asserting a single universal lineage.

In the received analysis of 愛, 夊 depicts slow or dragging walking, matching the gloss “appearance of walking”; 㤅 supplies the sound element. This is a historical analysis of 愛, not a role in current 爱.

overview.text: 爱 means “love” or “be fond of.” Its current form is 爫 above 冖 and 友; one proposed account traces the lower shape to joined or abbreviated 心-and-夂 strokes in running script.

components.text: 爫 is part of 爱’s visible upper structure; no historical function is established for it here.
冖 is the visible middle component in 爱; the evidence establishes its structure, not a separate historical role.
One proposed account of simplified 爱 traces its lower shape to joined or abbreviated 心-and-夂 strokes in running script; it does not give 友 an ancient role.

limitations.text: The early graphic of 愛 is described as 㤅, with later Qin-type forms including 夊, but the cited evidence does not establish one universal sequence or settle whether 㤅’s upper element is 兂 or 旡. Without a verified image of a specific form, its visible strokes cannot be illustrated reliably here.
